My dear Julian, you wear a brow furrowed with such admirable concern, one might conclude the very fabric of society had unravelled beneath your feet, or at the very least that my own fragile constitution had finally succumbed to the rigours of existence. But no, you see before you a man not merely intact, but, dare I say, revitalised. One cannot, after all, dwell upon the ephemeral tragedies of others with any degree of artistic integrity. You arrived, I presume, expecting tears, lamentations, perhaps even a suitable shade of crape for the draperies. How utterly charmingly sentimental of you.

“Arthur, you speak as if the recent incident were merely a minor inconvenience, a smudge on a perfectly polished silver tray. You cannot mean to suggest that Amelia’s sudden departure, or rather her abrupt dismissal from the household, leaves you entirely unmoved. The poor woman, after all, served your family for decades.”

Unmoved? My dear Julian, you misunderstand the very essence of human experience. I was, for a fleeting hour yesterday afternoon, quite consumed by a species of profound melancholy. Indeed, I found myself gazing at the newly acquired Venetian glass with a peculiar sense of shared fragility. But one cannot prolong such exquisite anguish; it becomes, eventually, merely a pose, a tiresome affectation. The true artist, and indeed the true man of feeling, acknowledges an emotion, savours its momentary intensity, and then, with admirable grace, permits it to recede. Only sentimentalists, those dreary souls who insist on rehearsing their sorrows like a badly written play, attempt to resurrect a sensation once it has passed. And besides, Amelia, bless her well-meaning but utterly prosaic soul, had begun to arrange the chrysanthemums with an almost offensive lack of asymmetry.

“Arthur, sometimes I fear for you. Your detachment, your pursuit of the purely aesthetic, will leave you quite alone one day, surrounded by beautiful objects and utterly devoid of human warmth. It is a dangerous path you tread, my friend, this constant striving to be the spectator of your own life, as that rather tedious Lord Alistair is so fond of proclaiming.”

And is not that precisely the point, Julian? To be alone, but beautifully so? To curate one’s existence as one would curate a gallery of the most exquisite masterpieces, free from the crude smudges of genuine human inconvenience? You, with your admirable but rather exhausting devotion to duty and human connection, miss the true exhilaration of objectivity. It is not coldness, I assure you, but clarity. Just this morning, while contemplating the subtle shift of light upon that rather magnificent jade carving, it occurred to me that emotion, raw and untamed, is merely an inferior form of pigment, suitable perhaps for the vulgar canvases of the masses, but quite unsuitable for the delicate miniature that is one’s soul. You are always so worried about my development, my dear Julian. You remember me from our days at Oxford, perhaps, when I still harboured the quaint notion that truth was somehow more compelling than beauty. I have grown, evolved. I am no longer that earnest undergraduate, but a connoisseur of existence, a collector of nuances, a sculptor of the self.

But come, my dear fellow, let us not waste this perfectly good afternoon on such tiresome dialectics. You must tell me what you think of my latest acquisition. I procured it from that rather dubious dealer in the Rue de Rivoli, a man with a suspiciously clean fingernail and an even more suspiciously antique snuff-box. It is a small, rather curious idol, said to be of pre-Columbian origin, though I suspect its true provenance lies more firmly in the workshops of some exceedingly clever Parisian forger. Still, its patina is exquisite. It sits, for the moment, behind that rather unassuming screen. Arthur gestured languidly with a hand adorned with several rings.

“You mean the screen you have drawn across the corner by the fireplace? I noticed it. I had thought you were simply attempting a new arrangement, or perhaps hiding some domestic transgression from my critical eye. But an idol? Let me see it, Arthur. You know how I appreciate your taste, even when it veers into the delightfully decadent.” Julian moved towards the screen.

Arthur’s voice sharpened, losing its languid tone. “No, Julian! You cannot look at it. I absolutely forbid it.” He stood abruptly, almost knocking over a delicate porcelain vase. His usual composure fractured, replaced by a sudden, intense pallor. His hands clenched slightly, and his eyes, usually so amused and distant, now held a sharp, almost desperate glint.

Julian paused, a hand outstretched towards the screen. “My dear Arthur, what is this melodramatic display? It is merely an idol, a piece of curiosa. I have seen your collection of medieval torture instruments, your rather unsettling Venetian masks. What could this possibly be that you guard it with such ferocious possessiveness?” He tried to peer around the edge.

“Do not touch that screen, Julian, I warn you. If you so much as lay a finger upon it, if you dare glimpse what lies beyond, then our friendship, our long and rather agreeable acquaintance, is at an end. I am entirely serious. There are things one does not share, even with those one professes to hold in the highest esteem. And I offer no explanations. You are merely to accept my decree.”

Julian stared at him, quite taken aback. He had never seen Arthur so agitated, so uncharacteristically raw in his display of emotion. Arthur, usually the very embodiment of controlled, elegant indifference, now trembled slightly. “Arthur, this is absurd. Quite absurd. You are behaving like a child who has hidden a particularly potent secret in his pocket. What possible harm could come from my seeing a mere idol? I thought you revelled in displaying your acquisitions, in shocking me with your latest aesthetic transgressions.” He took a step back, a cool displeasure in his tone. “I suppose you intend to exhibit this, this object, in your next salon, perhaps to scandalise the Duchess or provoke Professor Eldridge into another of his tiresome lectures on archaic symbolism.”

Arthur paled further, a bead of perspiration appearing on his brow. “Exhibit it! You imagine I would exhibit it?” His voice was a strained whisper, filled with a sudden, palpable terror. “No, Julian, never! The world must never see it. No one, not a single soul, must ever glimpse what lies behind that screen. It is private. It is mine. It is, it is altogether too potent for public consumption.” He ran a hand through his perfectly coiffed hair, his usual elegance quite abandoned.

“But you told me only last week, Arthur, when we were discussing the rather tiresome new trends in ethnographic art, that you were on the verge of acquiring something truly unique, something that would ‘redefine the very parameters of aesthetic appreciation,’ as you so grandly put it. You implied, quite strongly, that it would be the pièce de résistance of your next private viewing. You are, as ever, a creature of such delightful inconsistency. Or perhaps,” Julian’s eyes narrowed slightly, “perhaps Lord Fenwick was not entirely jesting when he suggested, at Lady Beaumont’s dreary soiree, that you always have a secret up your exquisitely tailored sleeve, a secret more intriguing than any of your public pronouncements.” He moved closer, a glint of determination in his eyes. “Tell me, Arthur, what is your secret? I have always shared my paltry indiscretions with you. Now, let me know yours. What is it that you truly hide behind that screen?”
